# fheatherx

Description: FheatherX is a private decentralized exchange built as a Uniswap v4 Hook using Fhenix's Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). FheatherXv6 combines a Hybrid Encrypted AMM with Private Limit Orders - supporting swaps and liquidity provision across ERC20 and FHERC20 token pairs
Tags: Custom hooks, DEX, LP Fees, LP Liquidity, MEV, Security
Integrations: Fhenix
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI7

# How did you integrate our partners, if any?

  FheatherX leverages Fhenix's Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to create the first truly private DEX where trade amounts, order sizes, and user balances remain encrypted on-chain. Using Fhenix's CoFHE protocol, we encrypt all sensitive values as euint128 types, enabling arithmetic operations like swaps (FHE.mul, FHE.div) and comparisons (FHE.gte, FHE.select) directly on encrypted data without ever revealing the underlying values. Our most innovative use of FHE is the "reverse tick calculation" for limit order triggering—instead of computing the current price tick (which would require sqrt and log operations unavailable in FHE), we check whether price crossed each order tick using the formula reserve1 >= tickPrice × reserve0, utilizing only FHE.mul and FHE.gte. Combined with FHE.xor for crossing detection and FHE.select for conditional execution, limit orders trigger synchronously during encrypted swaps without leaking whether any specific order was filled. This deep integration means
  MEV bots cannot see pending orders, frontrunners cannot detect large trades, and users enjoy complete financial privacy while still benefiting from the liquidity and composability of a Uniswap v4 hook.

# What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github:[https://github.com/daveaneo/pheatherx](https://github.com/daveaneo/pheatherx)
Slides: [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qWU5qnK9ZBEnYc8bbPZxc7qIsAMQZayd/view?usp=sharing](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1qWU5qnK9ZBEnYc8bbPZxc7qIsAMQZayd/view?usp=sharing)
Project Link:
Demo Video:[https://www.loom.com/share/805b3424a83640359637cc5311bbccd2](https://www.loom.com/share/805b3424a83640359637cc5311bbccd2)

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

FheatherX addresses four critical limitations that have prevented FHE-based DEXs from achieving production viability. First, we solve the O(N) scalability bottleneck—legacy encrypted orderbooks must blindly compare against every open order, causing transactions to run out of gas when liquidity grows; FheatherX uses tick-based bucketing to achieve O(1) constant-time matching regardless of order count. Second, we eliminate the "frozen market" problem where trades require off-chain keepers to trigger matching in separate transactions; our Uniswap V4 afterSwap hook atomically fills limit orders in the same transaction as the triggering swap, delivering "just-in-time" liquidity without external dependencies. Third, we introduce MEV protection via transient storage locks—even with encrypted amounts, bots can blindly sandwich trades, but FheatherX enforces unidirectional trading per transaction, making atomic sandwich attacks impossible and forcing attackers to take multi-block market risk.
  Finally, we break down the "walled garden" isolation of previous FHE DEXs that only support FHERC20 tokens; by building as a Uniswap V4 Hook, FheatherX pools are natively composable with the entire DeFi ecosystem, enabling single-transaction routes like ETH → USDC → private FHE-Token through the Universal Router.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

  FheatherX is the first DEX to combine Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Uniswap V4's hook architecture, creating a hybrid AMM + private limit order system where trade amounts, order sizes, and directions remain completely hidden on-chain. What makes it technically unique is our "reverse tick calculation"—since FHE lacks the sqrt and log operations needed to compute price ticks, we check whether price crossed each tick using only encrypted multiplication and comparison, enabling synchronous limit order execution without revealing which orders filled. The impact is significant: with over $1 billion lost annually to MEV sandwich attacks, FheatherX offers a path to dramatically reduce this extraction by making it impossible for bots to see order flow, size trades, or frontrun users. Traders gain true MEV immunity, market makers can place large orders without signaling intent, and the entire system plugs directly into Uniswap's ecosystem for seamless DeFi composability—proving that privacy and performance can coexist on public blockchains.

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

 Building FheatherX required overcoming obstacles at every layer of the stack. On the tooling side, Rainbow Wallet struggled with testnet compatibility, forcing us to build a custom development wallet, while acquiring testnet tokens proved frustratingly difficult. On the cryptographic side, FHE's limited math operations and inherently asynchronous decryption model created constant friction—requiring us to architect creative synchronous solutions for operations that typically demand waiting for off-chain computation to complete.

# FheMarket

Description: FheMarket is a privacy-first Uniswap V4 Hook that leverages Fhenix's Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to bring "Dark Pool" trading to DeFi. By enabling Shielded Deposits and Encrypted Swaps, it allows users to trade on prediction markets without revealing their position sizes, protecting them from front-running and copy-trading
Tags: Custom hooks, DEX, MEV, Security
Integrations: Fhenix
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)

# How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Partner: Fhenix

i integrated Fhenix to enable the "Dark Pool" privacy features of our Uniswap V4 Hook. Specifically, I utilized the Fhenix FHE.sol library interface to implement:

Encrypted Data Types: I replaced standard uint256 balances with euint128 (Encrypted Uint) to shield user funds from public view.

Blind Computation: I implemented FHE.add, FHE.sub, and FHE.select operations to perform accounting and trade logic on encrypted values without ever decrypting them on-chain.

Note: For this submission, i configured the project in a local "Simulation Mode." We imported the official Fhenix interfaces but used a local stub for the cryptographic operations. This ensures deterministic testing of the Uniswap V4 architecture and Hook logic without requiring judges to run a specialized FHE Docker node.

# What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github:[https://github.com/mandip-kamaliya/FheMarket](https://github.com/mandip-kamaliya/FheMarket)
Slides: 
Project Link:
Demo Video:[https://www.loom.com/share/461ad930d1b44174a568fb9e81f80037](https://www.loom.com/share/461ad930d1b44174a568fb9e81f80037)

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

I was inspired by the concept of "Dark Pools" in traditional finance, where institutional traders can place large orders without revealing their hand to the market.

In current DeFi prediction markets (like Polymarket), every trade and position size is fully visible on-chain. This transparency creates a critical problem: Information Leakage. If a "whale" or institution tries to take a large position, the market reacts instantly, leading to:

Front-running & MEV: Bots detect the large buy and trade against it.

Copy-Trading: Competitors can instantly mimic proprietary strategies.

Slippage: The public visibility moves the price before the trade settles.

I built FheMarket to solve this by introducing Shielded Liquidity to Uniswap V4. By using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), I created a system where users can deposit funds and execute swaps while keeping their balance and bet size completely encrypted, protecting their strategy from public view while maintaining on-chain integrity.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

What makes this project unique? Most privacy tools are just mixers; my project delivers Privacy-Preserving Utility. I built a functional "Dark Pool" on Uniswap V4 where the ledger itself is encrypted. By combining Uniswap hooks with Fhenix’s blind computation, I enable complex financial operations on shielded assets, something previously impossible on standard EVM chains.

What impact will this make? FheMarket solves the "Confidentiality Gap" keeping institutions out of DeFi. By eliminating front-running and copy-trading, it allows whales to enter on-chain markets without revealing their hand. This proves that sensitive financial data can exist on a public blockchain without exposure, paving the way for institutional-grade, compliant DeFi.

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The biggest challenge was the incompatibility between standard Foundry testing and the specialized FHE precompiles required by Fhenix. The local Docker node was unstable for rapid iteration, often reverting on valid encrypted operations which made debugging the logic nearly impossible.

I overcame this by architecting a custom Simulation Stub. Instead of fighting the infrastructure, I reversed-engineered the Fhenix interface and wrote a local library that mimics the FHE operations using standard math. This allowed me to verify the Uniswap V4 permissions and hook logic deterministically, ensuring the architecture was solid without relying on the fragile local node.

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gLvxDolhLY8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gLvxDolhLY8)

### **Description**

Attracts swappers with fee discounts based on the volume they generate. Operates as a system where the liquidity of Liquidity Providers (LPs) is retained for the entire duration of a configurable cycle set at the pool's initialization (e.g., one week). Tokenizes swappers' "loyalty" by issuing fungible tokens that represent the volume a swapper has generated, making them eligible for discounts. Once obtained, these loyalty tokens can be used to receive trading fee discounts, as if the volume was generated by the token holder. Brevis is used to regularly update trading volume metrics.

### **Challenges**

First challenge was to find a mechanism to disallow LPs to "run off" with the liquidity once swappers would slowly start to reach better than market fee percentages -> that's how we've come to the conclusion that campaigns that last a certain amount of time in which LPs lock their liquidity would mitigate this issue.
We've also tried to integrate our hook with the Uniswap frontend but did not manage to fully integrate it.
We initially had the idea of an optional Brevis plugin to track infidelity, meaning swaps across external pools, and penalize the swappers by reducing their accumulated fee percentages, however one could easily send tokens to another wallet for swapping outside the fidelity-hook enabled pool. We ended up implementing a Brevis solution that focuses on overall volume of a certain token across all pools.
The biggest challenge was to allow LPs to recenter their positions - this wasn't technically straightforward, as we had to take the liquidity modification logic inside our Hook by implementing functions to add/remove/recenter liquidity.

### **Contributions**

I've written the overall logic of the hook contract.
Alex Males handled the Brevis related part.
Catalin Balut came up with fidelity tokens concept and contributed to the implementation + wrote tests.
George Negru and Sergiu Corches also wrote tests.
The whole team regularly met for discussions on how to shape the hook.

# Firstless

Description: Firstless gives an exact-output trader the requested tokens immediately, but waits until the block is complete before fixing the input bill. It nets opposite orders first, charges each order for the extra cost it added, and returns unused maximum input as a backed refund.
Tags: CFMM, DEX, LP Fees, MEV, Order Type, Security
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI3

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

I deployed Firstless on Unichain Sepolia with the official Uniswap v4 PoolManager. The dashboard uses real contracts throughout. A wallet can claim test tokens, sign an exact-output order, and receive output in the same transaction. After the canonical block closes, it can settle the order and redeem the refund. I also tested the pending-to-active LP flow.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/aryan877/firstless](https://github.com/aryan877/firstless)
Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1vKffVTG0HPjc7O5joL5mRtsL78ri4jKJ/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=102837795620539328319&rtpof=true&sd=true
Project Link: https://firstless.aryankumar.dev
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/dUv3-BieBWs](https://youtu.be/dUv3-BieBWs)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

On a normal AMM, transaction order can change who pays what. Eve can buy before Alice, let Alice move the price, then sell after her. Alice pays more because of where her transaction landed. I built Firstless to give Alice her exact output immediately while waiting until the block is complete to calculate her final input bill.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Firstless separates delivery from billing. Traders receive their output inside the signed transaction, while same-block orders can net before the hook calculates each order's marginal cost. In 39 pinned Ethereum sandwich replays, 37 attacker portfolios made money under sequential execution and none made money in the Firstless model I tested. This result only covers those complete same-set sandwich cases. It does not mean Firstless stops every kind of MEV.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hardest part was delivering the output immediately without treating the maximum input as the final price. I had to keep refunds fully backed, separate refund liabilities from LP funds, handle integer rounding, and stop new liquidity from earning old fees. I covered these cases with adversarial tests, fuzzing, and stateful invariants. I also ran 39 pinned sandwich replays, local end-to-end demos, and the Unichain Sepolia lifecycle.

# Fixed-Income Tranche Hook

Description: Fixed-Income Tranche Hook brings structured finance to Uniswap v4 by splitting LP capital into senior and junior ERC-20 tranches. Senior LPs receive fixed-priority yield, while junior LPs absorb impermanent loss and fee shortfalls in exchange for residual upside, with epoch settlement automated through Reactive Network.
Tags: Aave Adapter, ERC-20 Tranche Tokens, Epoch Settlement, Fixed Income, Impermanent Loss, LP Tranching, RSC, Reactive Network, Senior/Junior Liquidity, Structured Products, Uniswap v4 Hook, Yield Systems
Integrations: Reactive Network
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI9

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

The project integrates Reactive Network through a Reactive Smart Contract deployed on Lasna. The hook emits FeesAccrued(uint256,uint256,uint256) events, the RSC subscribes to those events, checks whether the epoch is mature, and emits a callback to settleEpochFromReactive(address,uint256) on the Unichain Sepolia hook. The hook authenticates the callback with both msg.sender == callbackProxy and sender == reactiveSender.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/KHRAFTSng/fixed-income-tranche-hook](https://github.com/KHRAFTSng/fixed-income-tranche-hook)
Slides: https://gamma.app/docs/Fixed-Income-Tranche-Hook-zfa2dvhfiwsn5b9
Project Link: 
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/w9NdbVxpj2g](https://youtu.be/w9NdbVxpj2g)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Uniswap LPs currently face one undifferentiated risk profile: every LP absorbs the same fee volatility and impermanent loss regardless of whether they want predictable yield or higher-risk upside. That makes v4 pools harder to use for allocators who need fixed-income-like exposure and for risk-seeking LPs who want explicit levered upside. Fixed-Income Tranche Hook solves this by creating a capital structure inside a v4 pool: senior LPs are paid first, while junior LPs intentionally absorb IL and shortfalls in return for residual fee upside.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

This project is unique because it turns LP positions into explicit senior and junior ERC-20 tranche tokens with deterministic waterfall accounting. Instead of only adjusting fees or routing idle capital, it assigns risk to the users who choose to take it: senior LPs get fixed-priority yield, and junior LPs receive the upside after senior obligations are paid. The impact is a new LP primitive for Uniswap v4 that can support fixed-income products, structured vaults, risk-segmented liquidity markets, and more institutional-friendly liquidity provisioning.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hardest part was making the Reactive integration provable end-to-end rather than treating it as a black-box callback. The system needed to prove the origin FeesAccrued event, the Lasna RSC subscription and ReactVM logic, the destination callback proxy call, and the final EpochSettled event. Another challenge was keeping the tranche accounting deterministic and testable: senior payout priority, junior shortfall absorption, IL attribution, same-epoch withdrawal protection, and callback idempotency all needed explicit tests.

# FlexFee

Description: Protecting LPs from impermanent loss using dynamic fees based on volatility (calculated with Brevis) and swap size
Integrations: Brevis, EigenLayer
Cohort: UHI1
Prize: Brevis Prize

<aside>
🦄 Protecting LPs from impermanent loss using dynamic fees based on volatility (calculated with Brevis) and swap size.

</aside>

<aside>
🔗 **Links**

- [Slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1hljfF7fZexpF8SzpuALGzGznb1RqF4_O2URXzJOWYpo)
- [GitHub](https://github.com/Decentralisedme/uhi_flexfee)
</aside>

### Demo:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZU8osonTsqY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZU8osonTsqY)

### **Description**

In order book based exchanges liquidity providers are able to compensate for and deter trades that incur loss by increasing fees via bid/ask spreads. We have implemented a Uniswap V4 Hook that offers this protection to liquidity providers by dynamically adjusting fees so that higher fees are charged during periods of high volatility and when filling large swaps. 

The on-chain calculation of realized volatility based on historical prices is computationally expensive (and infeasible due to gas costs). This, however, would be a perfect use-case for the Brevis co-processor. We have created a Brevis circuit for calculating realized volatility along with a corresponding ZK proof. The expensive volatility computation is now performed off-chain, and the results together with a ZK proof of the input price data and the calculation is then written on-chain. The Brevis service feeds updated verified volatility values into our hook contract via a callback function. 

Our hook implements the beforeSwap function and returns an override fee which is calculated based on the latest volatility and the size of the current swap. We have various unit tests that demonstrate how the fee increased in relation to high volatility and large swap sizes.

Our inspiration for the project was taken from our TradeFi experience in seeing how markets react to volatility (we are a team of ex-TradFi quant traders and devs).

There were some connectivity issues with the Brevis service and some of the Brevis code example repos were out of date. However, the Brevis team was very helpful and responsive on Discord. 

Also we had to refactor our hook to account for changes to the Uniswap v4-core repository, however Haardik helped us resolve these.

### **Contributions**

There was a lot of overlap and paired programming with team members. The general work split is as follows:

Howell: research using Binance data into how order books price in volatility and order size. Research and implementation of fee calculation in Solidity.

Rayan: realized volatility Brevis circuit in Go using Brevis SDK. Service application for continuously calculating and publishing up-to-date volatilities using TypeScript.

Riccardo: development of testing of dynamic fee hook using Uniswap v4-core repo in Solidity.

James: development of hook callback function for receiving updated verified volatility data from Brevis in Solidity.  Also some project management.

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

FlowAid addresses the systemic issue of period poverty affecting millions of girls across Africa where lack of access to basic menstrual hygiene products directly undermines education, health, and dignity.

In many underserved communities, girls face impossible trade-offs, sometimes resorting to exploitative means to access sanitary products, exposing them to risks such as early pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections. On average, this results in the loss of up to 4–5 days of school every month, compounding into long-term educational and economic disadvantage.

Despite the scale of the problem, existing interventions remain fragmented, donation-dependent, and difficult to verify leaving a critical gap in consistent, transparent, and sustainable support systems.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

FlowAid's paradigm shift from episodic giving to programmable, perpetual funding. Rather than relying on voluntary donations, I introduce an embedded impact layer within liquidity flows themselves.

This project redefines DeFi infrastructure as a vehicle for public goods by:

Converting every swap into a micro-contribution without disrupting user behavior

Ensuring full onchain transparency and verifiability, eliminating trust gaps

Creating a scalable, borderless funding mechanism for underserved communities

The impact is twofold:

Immediate — consistent funding streams for schools, improving attendance and dignity for girls

Systemic — establishing a new financial primitive where markets inherently fund social good

FlowAidHooks demonstrates that impact can be native to protocols, not an afterthought.

One of the most significant challenges was designing a system that balances technical precision with real-world usability.

On the protocol side, integrating seamlessly with Uniswap v4 hooks particularly the afterSwap lifecycle required careful handling of fee routing logic to ensure accuracy, efficiency, and composability without breaking core swap functionality.

On the application layer, I tackled the challenge of trust-minimized fund distribution, implementing signature-based withdrawals to ensure that only verified schools can access funds while maintaining decentralization principles.

Additionally, aligning blockchain mechanics with a real-world impact use case required thoughtful abstraction ensuring that complex infrastructure translates into intuitive, meaningful outcomes for non-crypto-native beneficiaries.

# FlowPass

Description: FlowPass is a Uniswap v4 fee-smoothing yield hook that sells prepaid trading passes: traders pay upfront for discounted future swap volume, and the hook tracks quota and expiry per wallet. The pass revenue is split into LP reserve and treasury revenue, while the discount helps retain recurring order flow in competitive pools.
Tags: DEX, LP Fees, LP Liquidity, Trading Volume Rewards
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI9

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/Joezhouzmz/FlowPass](https://github.com/Joezhouzmz/FlowPass)
Slides: 
Project Link: https://flowpass.joezhouzmz.workers.dev/
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/ft2iuAvbOCg](https://youtu.be/ft2iuAvbOCg)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

In highly competitive pools, especially stablecoin-style routing markets, traders can choose between many similar venues. Prices, liquidity, fees, and routing are extremely transparent, and traders can switch pools with very low friction. A simple fee discount may attract flow, but it can also reduce LP revenue if the same flow would have stayed anyway.

FlowPass is inspired by Costco-style membership economics: a user pays upfront, then receives lower prices later. The merchant may earn less per transaction, but the membership creates commitment, repeat usage, and higher total volume. FlowPass applies this idea to AMMs by asking recurring traders to prepay for a time-limited discounted quota, giving them a reason to keep routing through the FlowPass pool.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

FlowPass turns swap-fee competition into a yield product and business model. Traders get lower marginal execution costs after buying a pass, LPs get discounted swap fees plus an upfront reserve allocation, and the protocol captures prepaid revenue through the hook treasury.

The project also shows why hooks matter commercially, not only technically. In a transparent AMM market, purely technical advantages can be copied or arbitraged away. FlowPass creates pool-level differentiation through prepaid access, quota, expiry, and revenue sharing. It also gives hook creators a path to sustainable treasury revenue, which can help incentivize more serious mechanism design in the Uniswap v4 hook ecosystem.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hardest parts were translating a membership-pass model into real Uniswap v4 hook mechanics, handling dynamic LP fee overrides correctly, and avoiding quota mis-accounting around swaps. The MVP also needed a custom exact-input router so the hook could receive trader identity in hookData, plus a clear explanation of why standard router quoting does not automatically understand pass discounts.

# FlowShield

Description: A Uniswap v4 hook that turns MEV into LP yield, and makes sandwich attacks structurally impossible built entirely on native v4 primitives.
Tags: MEV
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI7

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/Amity808/FlowShield](https://github.com/Amity808/FlowShield)
Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1R7zAij6PoKoD2DoYHDwbfFFD-8iIHCwf/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=103170431718300742214&rtpof=true&sd=true
Project Link: 
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/d7GmDE1pzkk](https://youtu.be/d7GmDE1pzkk)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

I kept coming back to the same observation from prior hookathon builds: volatile-pair liquidity on Uniswap is structurally unprofitable, and it's not one problem. it's three compounding ones. Sandwich attacks skim 0.3–1.5% off retail swappers and train pools to expect toxic flow. LVR quietly bleeds LPs every time the off-chain price moves before the pool catches up. And a flat fee can't tell the difference between an arbitrageur exploiting a stale price and a retail trader just moving tokens so LPs get paid the same tiny amount for both, which is really underpaid for the first and overpriced for the second. Most hooks I'd seen picked one of these three to solve. I wanted to know whether a single hook could address all three at once, since they're not actually independent MEV, sandwiching, and mispriced flow all come from the same root cause: the pool has no way to tell who it's dealing with before the trade executes.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

FlowShield combines three mechanisms that, as far as I can tell, no other v4 hook runs together: commit-reveal sandwich protection, an on-chain MEV auction, and toxic/healthy flow-based dynamic fees all native to v4's hook callbacks and dynamic-fee system, with no off-chain relayer or oracle. The auction piece is the part I'm most proud of: instead of MEV leaking to searchers and validators, the first-swap-of-block right is auctioned on-chain, and FlowShieldRouter makes the bid and the swap atomic in a single transaction, so a losing bid can never get stranded and nobody can free-ride on someone else's payment. The impact, if this pattern holds up: LPs on volatile pairs stop subsidizing arbitrageurs and sandwichers and start getting paid for the risk they're actually carrying, which is the difference between volatile-pair liquidity being a losing bet and a sustainable one.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The biggest one was realizing my first design was lying to itself. I'd built the MEV auction so the bid and the swap were two separate calls in the "same block" which sounds atomic but isn't: nothing stopped another transaction from landing in between, and nothing tied the winning bid to the swap that actually consumed it. Catching that gap meant redesigning the entry point as a router that bundles both into one transaction, so an underbid reverts everything, bid included, instead of leaving it stranded. A related constraint: v4 hook callbacks are invoked as plain external calls with no msg.value forwarded, so there's no way for a bid to arrive "inside" beforeSwap no matter how it's designed that's a real limitation of the hook architecture, not a bug to fix.

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Fluidity solves two key problems in DeFi: strategy privacy and liquidity rebalancing. 

1. Sensitive strategy parameters (price thresholds, rebalancing logic, position sizes) are visible in smart contract storage and events, allowing bots to analyze and replicate successful strategies. 
2. Manual liquidity management is inefficient. Positions need constant rebalancing to maintain optimal capital efficiency. Fluidity addresses both by encrypting strategy configurations using FHE to prevent analysis, while providing automated rebalancing that works on encrypted data, maintaining full Uniswap V4 compatibility.

Uniswap V4 hook to combine FHE with automated liquidity rebalancing for MEV protection and optimal capital efficiency.

# FLUXA

Description: Fluxa is the first Uniswap v4 hook purpose-built for RWA exit liquidity. The tokenized RWA market is $38B and growing — but when LPs need to exit before maturity, their capital is trapped. Goldfinch FIDU has a 1-year withdrawal queue at 100% utilization. Tags: Auctions, Constant Sum Market Maker (CSMM), Custom hooks, DEX, Dynamic Fee, Illiquid Assets, LP Fees, LP Liquidity, MEV, Machine Learning, Oracle, Price Discovery, Private Debt, RWA, Reputation
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI10

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

EigenLayer — Fluxa integrates EigenLayer AVS as a validation gate for AI agent decisions in Mode B (AI-inferred pricing for illiquid RWA assets).
How it works:
1. On-chain validation (FluxaHook.sol): During every Mode B swap, the hook calls avsValidator.validateDecision(agentId, keccak256(aiPrice), proof) after the TEE attestation is verified. If AVS rejects → the swap falls back to Mode A (Chronicle oracle price). If AVS approves → the swap executes at the AI-inferred price.
2. Smart contract (MockEigenLayerAVS.sol): Deployed on Base Sepolia at 0xD604fA15Ee7217F0238471F56bc8da703E19c27c. Implements IEigenLayerAVS interface with validateDecision() returning a boolean + reason string. Operator-set allowlist controls which agent IDs are permitted.
3. Hook wiring: The hook owner calls setAVSValidator(avsAddress) to wire the AVS contract. Setting address(0) disables validation (optional). Agent ID=1 is already allowed in the deployed instance.
4. Frontend: The AgentTab in the pool detail page displays real-time AVS validation status (allowed/not allowed) by reading MockEigenLayerAVS.allowedAgents(agentId) on-chain.
5. Tests: 12 AgentLayer tests passing, including AVS rejection scenarios that verify the fallback to Mode A oracle pricing.
In short: EigenLayer AVS acts as a slashing gate for the AI agent — if the validator rejects the agent's pricing decision, the hook automatically falls back to oracle-based pricing, ensuring integrity of the AI pricing pipeline.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/Shenhan01-sys/fluxa-fe ; https://github.com/Shenhan01-sys/fluxa-hook](https://github.com/Shenhan01-sys/fluxa-fe ; https://github.com/Shenhan01-sys/fluxa-hook)
Slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1-67yRjSTPAbGynvpL3pRpexRsDDtSq2D/view?usp=drive_link
Project Link: http://fluxa-weld.vercel.app/
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/2yY_QweTlko](https://youtu.be/2yY_QweTlko)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) have grown to a $38B market with 1.79M holders, but they share a fundamental flaw: there is no exit door. Bonds, invoices, and real estate positions are illiquid by nature. When LPs need to exit before maturity, the only option is a fire-sale OTC trade at 20-40% discounts. Traditional DEXs use x*y=k pricing which fails when one side has no natural demand. Goldfinch FIDU has a 1-year withdrawal queue with 100% utilization — capital is effectively trapped. We were inspired by this gap: RWA vaults need purpose-built liquidity infrastructure that can price illiquid assets fairly and provide instant exit.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Fluxa is the first Uniswap v4 hook built specifically for RWA exit liquidity. What makes it unique is the three-mode auto-routing system: Mode A (oracle yield routing for liquid RWAs via Chronicle), Mode B (AI-inferred pricing for illiquid RWAs via Groq LLM + TEE attestation + EigenLayer AVS validation), and Mode C (sealed-bid auction for distress liquidation). The hook reads pool state on every swap and routes automatically — no off-chain coordinator, no multisig, pure on-chain logic. This creates a complete lifecycle: deposit USDC, earn yield, and exit instantly at any time — even when the underlying asset has no public market. The agent layer (ERC-8004 reputation, ERC-7857 NFT identity, x402 streaming payments) makes this a fully autonomous pricing pipeline from LLM inference to on-chain settlement.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The biggest challenge was getting Uniswap v4 PoolManager integration right — the unlock callback pattern, CurrencySettler library, and ERC-6909 claim token accounting required deep understanding of v4 internals. We went through 5 deploy iterations (v1→v5) after discovering the PoolManager address was incorrect on one attempt, which silently broke all pool interactions. Another challenge was the Mode B attestation pipeline: encoding a 160-byte TEE-mock proof (agentId + priceWei + timestamp + enclaveHash + signature), passing it through hookData, and decoding it via assembly calldataload inside the hook. The dynamic fee calculation also required careful math — BASE_FEE + riskTier × 10bps — while keeping the poolKey fee at 0 (hook-managed, not PM-managed, which caused a poolId mismatch bug where the frontend computed the wrong pool ID and all addLiquidity transactions reverted).

Architecturally, the project runs across two tiers: the frontend is deployed on Vercel (https://fluxa-weld.vercel.app/) for public access, while the AI agent service runs locally on port 3030 because it requires a private key to register attestations on-chain and call the Groq LLM API. The Vercel frontend reads pool data directly from Base Sepolia via public RPC (no backend needed), but the Mode B "Compute Fair Price" and "Build Attestation" buttons require the local agent service to be running. For the demo, both the Vercel frontend and the local agent service are used simultaneously. Finally, building a full-stack autonomous agent system (LLM → attestation → AVS → on-chain swap → x402 payment → reputation feedback) across 7 contracts, an off-chain service, and a frontend in 15 days was intense.

# FluxShield - Adaptive fee hook for UniswapV4

Description: FluxShield is an adaptive fee hook for Uniswap v4 that uses Chainlink price feeds to detect market‑AMM deviation and dynamically escalates swap fees, protecting liquidity providers from arbitrage extraction while preserving price synchronization
Tags: Dynamic Fee, LP Fees, LVR
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI9
Date: June 8, 2026

### **Key Links**

- **GitHub:** [https://github.com/ighodaro-daniel/fluxshieldHook](https://github.com/ighodaro-daniel/fluxshieldHook)
- **Demo Video:** [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6YfT3vvpd7g](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6YfT3vvpd7g)

### **Partner Integrations**

No partner integrations.

### **Problem / Background**

The idea for FluxShield came from observing a fundamental imbalance in AMM design: LPs absorb most of the downside from arbitrage-driven inventory shifts, yet fee structures treat all swaps equally. During periods of high volatility, stale AMM prices become hunting grounds for arbitrageurs who extract value that rightfully belongs to LPs.

Existing solutions either eliminate arbitrage entirely (which breaks price synchronization) or rely on static fees that cannot adapt to market stress. The question: can we build a fee mechanism that scales with arbitrage risk, protecting LPs without destroying market efficiency? Problems addressed: Loss-Versus-Rebalancing (LVR), Static Fee Inefficiency, Oracle Misalignment.

### **Impact**

FluxShield is the first v4 hook that integrates Chainlink directly into fee determination — fees respond to real-time market divergence, not just on-chain liquidity conditions. The configurable, non-linear fee curve lets owners tune thresholds and fee tiers to balance LP protection vs. arbitrage incentive. Crucially, FluxShield preserves arbitrage — unlike aggressive anti-MEV designs, it keeps arbitrage profitable enough to maintain price sync, simply taxing it more fairly.

### **Challenges**

Initially used the Pyth oracle to fetch price data, but encountered a problem: every swap required the swapper to pay an additional fee to update and retrieve the latest price. Ultimately switched to the Chainlink oracle, which provides price feed access without imposing per-swap costs on users.

# ForgeX: Vult

Description: ForgeX:Vult is a yield-native hook that puts idle LP capital to work, it routes liquidity into ERC-4626 vaults (Aave +   Compound) and then donates the accrued interest back to LPs after every swap. So LPs are just earning swap fees and lending   yield at the same time, automatically, no extra steps needed.
Tags: Constant Product Market Maker (CPMM), Custom hooks, DEX, LP Fees, LP Liquidity, RWA, Stablecoins, Yield Farming
Integrations: Unichain
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI8

# How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Partner Integration: Unichain

ForgeX integrates with Uniswap v4 through a custom hook system called VultHook, which implements the IHooks interface and connects to key events like afterAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, and afterSwap.

When liquidity is added, idle capital is automatically routed into ERC-4626 vaults and deployed into Aave V3 and Compound V2 to generate yield. During swaps, liquidity remains available, and any accrued yield is harvested and redistributed to LPs using poolManager.donate().

Chainlink Price Feeds provide real-time asset valuation, while Chainlink Automation enables periodic yield harvesting and rebalancing.

Deployed on Base, this architecture allows LPs to earn both trading fees and DeFi yield, transforming passive liquidity into an active, yield-generating strategy.

# What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/BitBand-Labs/forgeX](https://github.com/BitBand-Labs/forgeX)
Slides: [https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1BxzJ7kp0T9UA092X6j3Rze7UmorCeSYA/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=100528488557506058575&rtpof=true&sd=true](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1BxzJ7kp0T9UA092X6j3Rze7UmorCeSYA/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=100528488557506058575&rtpof=true&sd=true)
Project Link:[https://forgex-vult.vercel.app/](https://forgex-vult.vercel.app/)
Demo Video:[https://docs.google.com/document/d/189oCgRl9NN3FPlATtben9-FJdBpW6QirQZvo_Coo3aY/edit?usp=drive_link](https://docs.google.com/document/d/189oCgRl9NN3FPlATtben9-FJdBpW6QirQZvo_Coo3aY/edit?usp=drive_link)

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Honestly, the thing that got me thinking about this was just ,why is all this LP capital sitting there doing nothing between trades? Like there's literally billions of dollars in AMM pools that earn zero lending yield because it's just waiting. Every time there's no swap happening, that capital is just idle. That felt like such an obvious gap.

So the idea was: what if the hook could just quietly put that money to work in lending protocols while nobody's using it, and then return the yield to the LPs automatically? No new token, no governance overhead, no user action required. Just more yield on top of what LPs were already earning.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Most yield hooks I've seen either redirect fees or require LPs to opt into some separate system. ForgeX actually deploys the underlying capital , not just the fees into Aave and Compound, which means the yield base is much larger. And the whole thing runs at the hook level, so it works for any LP in any pool that uses VultHook, not just people who know to sign up for something.

On top of the hook, we built a full personal vault system with an AI strategy engine (Claude Sonnet) that gives users actual insight into their positions yield %, risk score, allocation advice. I think that's the part that makes it feel like a real product and not just a smart contract demo.

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

 The hook architecture took some getting used to honestly. Making sure the hook address had the right permission bits set, and handling the balance delta correctly in afterAddLiquidity without breaking the pool invariants that took a few iterations.

The other tricky part was the yield detection in afterSwap. You can't just check accrued yield naively because Compound's balanceOfUnderlying is state-modifying, so we had to be careful about when and how we call it inside a hook context.

On the frontend side, the portfolio page was a bit of a challenge you can't call useVaultData in a loop because of React hooks rules, so we ended up building a VaultDataCollector component pattern to accumulate data across vaults cleanly.

Our team consists of two developers working on DeFi infrastructure.

myself (Babalola) -  Lead Developer: Responsible for protocol design, smart contract development, and implementing the hook-based yield architecture.

(Nonso) – Security & Integrations Engineer: Focused on smart contract auditing, security review, and integration with external DeFi protocols.

# FrontrunThis

Description: FrontrunThis is a privacy-focused trading layer built on Uniswap v4, powered by EigenLayer and EigenDA. It enables encrypted trade matching off-chain and secure on-chain settlement, protecting users from MEV like frontrunning and sandwich attacks.
Tags: Cross-Chain, Custom hooks, Dark Pools, ETH Staking, MEV, Security
Integrations: EigenLayer
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI5
Prize: EigenLayer Prize, Uniswap Prize

# How did you integrate our partners, if any?

we integrated eigenlayer and eigenDA to make frontrunthis truly mev-resistant. our custom AVS is built on eigenlayer and handles the private matching of trade orders off-chain. when users submit orders, they don’t go to the public mempool. instead, they’re encrypted and sent directly to the AVS. the AVS matches buy and sell orders privately and posts the encrypted batch to eigenda, a decentralized data availability layer. this ensures the trade data is safely stored but hidden from mev bots until it’s time to settle. after a short delay, the AVS reveals the batch and submits it to a uniswap v4 hook, where the trades are executed on-chain. this prevents frontrunning and sandwich attacks because no one sees the trades until they’ve already been matched and finalized. eigenlayer gives our AVS a decentralized trust model using staked validators, and eigenDA guarantees that data is available and untampered

# What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github:[https://github.com/rahulbarmann/FrontrunThis](https://github.com/rahulbarmann/FrontrunThis)
Slides: [https://www.canva.com/design/DAGrgM3ojxo/6LpzQLaGpy75JUHE_Lt2Fg/edit?utm_content=DAGrgM3ojxo&amp;utm_campaign=designshare&amp;utm_medium=link2&amp;utm_source=sharebutton](https://www.canva.com/design/DAGrgM3ojxo/6LpzQLaGpy75JUHE_Lt2Fg/edit?utm_content=DAGrgM3ojxo&utm_campaign=designshare&utm_medium=link2&utm_source=sharebutton)
Project Link:

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

We got frontrun. A couple of times.

Trades are visible before they execute giving MEV bots a chance to frontrun or sandwich them for profit. That’s unfair and frustrating. Our solution matches trades privately using a custom EigenLayer AVS, encrypts them, and only reveals them after consensus via EigenDA. Settlement happens through Uniswap v4 Hooks, keeping it trustless and composable.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

We stop bots from seeing and exploiting your trade before it happens. In normal DeFi trading, bots watch the mempool and jump in front of your transaction or sandwich it to make money leaving you with worse prices. We prevent that by keeping your trade private until it’s too late for bots to act. Orders are matched off-chain, encrypted, and only revealed at the moment of execution. This removes any chance for frontrunning or sandwiching

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

Our biggest challenge was avoiding the AMM price updates, which MEV bots use to frontrun trades. To fix this, we had to design a way to match and agree on trade prices off-chain before sending anything to Uniswap. This meant stepping away from normal AMM flow and figuring out how to settle trades at pre-agreed prices, while still using Uniswap v4 for final execution.

### **Description**

This project enables depositing in specific ranges via the hook contract. With those ranges made fungible by minting LP tokens to users based on liquidity provided. All liquidity will be owned by the hook and the LP tokens will represent the share of that liquidity for each range. Each range will be linked to two staking contracts for the LP tokens and two Vaults, one for each token of the pool. The staking contracts will allow to claim the fees generated by the pool, and the Vaults will invest out of range liquidity in the strategy defined in the specific vault. This would especially work well for stable pools, as most users are willing to invest in smaller or larger ranges depending on the volatility they expect between those stable tokens. And liquidity would constantly be generating yield, through fees in the pool when range is active and  and yield from the vaults when inactive. It also allows to easily incentivize LP'ing in specific ranges by sending reward tokens to the staking contracts. Also note that on each modifyLiquidity , the fees accumulated are accounted and sent to staking contract before a change in totalSupply of LP tokens.

Regarding the Vaults, those are ERC4626 slightly modified to account for the shares of the specific ranges. Currenty those are linked to a mocked Aave pool but could be any strategy generating yield.

Main challenge was to adapt to UniswapV4 codebase. Went a few times back to the lessons we had and also by going through UniswapV4 testing files I could see how everything was put together and helped.

Maintaing all accounting of the different ranges through the Vault/Hook/Staking contract was a challenge and had to refactor the code multiple times.

# FxHedgeHook — Delta-Neutral IL Shield for a FX Yield Machine

Description:   FxHedgeHook is a Uniswap v4 hook that tracks LP exposure on FX/BTC pools in real time and   auto-opens offsetting short perps on our on-chain clearinghouse, neutralizing impermanent   loss so LPs keep the full spread + yield. It's the IL shield of a larger "yield machine"   where empty-pool delta-accounting (FxSwapHook) lets the same capital earn Morpho/USYC yield   between swaps.
Tags: Cross-Chain, DEX, Dynamic Fee, Inter-Connected Pools, LP Liquidity, LVR, Options/Futures, Stablecoins
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI9

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Circle - past cohort it seems.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/BuFi007/fx-telarana](https://github.com/BuFi007/fx-telarana)
Slides: 
Project Link: https://fx.bu.finance
Demo Video: [https://video.bu.finance/video/bufx-multi-chain-forex-and-defi-protocol-1-ch68](https://video.bu.finance/video/bufx-multi-chain-forex-and-defi-protocol-1-ch68)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

LPs on volatile pairs (BTC/USDC, FX/USDC) bleed impermanent loss that routinely exceeds fee income — “yield” that ends up net negative. Meanwhile, their capital sits idle in pools between swaps, earning nothing.

We built both halves:

FxHedgeHook measures each pool’s directional exposure on every swap and liquidity event using EMA TWAP and a 2% deviation circuit breaker. It emits hedge deltas that automatically open offsetting shorts on our on-chain perp clearinghouse, deleting the IL drag.

FxSwapHook serves swaps via `beforeSwapReturnDelta` from an oracle-anchored PMM with empty pools. That means the backing capital is not trapped in passive liquidity. It earns Morpho lending APY and a USYC T-bill floor until the instant a swap summons it.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

LP yield becomes honest: spread, perp-fee share, and money-market yield, with impermanent loss hedged instead of ignored.

The empty-pool design means a single vault deposit can back every FX pool, with no fragmented ranges. Tranche accounting protects senior lenders by making the junior buffer absorb money-market PnL first, while a hard on-chain compliance wall keeps retail NAV out of Reg-S USYC.

Everything self-operates through permissionless, incentivized `rebalance()`, with no off-chain SaaS in the value path.

Live across two Gateway-bridged hubs — Fuji and Arc — with eight CCTP spokes.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hardest parts were:

1. Hedge sizing without oracle manipulation. We solved this with per-pool EMA TWAP and auto-pause on 2% deviation. On Arc, there is a single oracle, so circuit breakers are load-bearing.

2. Keeping the swap hot path sacred. Hedging and yield movement are fully out-of-band. `beforeSwap` stays under 50k gas with a single vault call.

3. Decimal hell. Arc has 18-decimal native gas USDC, 6-decimal ERC-20 USDC, 8-decimal cirBTC, and 18-decimal JPYC.

4. Enforcing the retail/USYC compliance wall as an on-chain invariant. `retailAssets ∩ USYC = ∅` is enforced in code, not treated as a policy note.

5. Cross-hub capital that is never idle. Gateway burn-intents are EOA-signed until Circle ships ERC-1271, so we designed authority rotation in advance.

# Gacha Hook

Description: The Gacha Hook addresses high entry barriers, illiquidity, and inefficient revenue models in the NFT market by enabling fractionalization and cross-chain support for a more accessible and dynamic trading experience.

</aside>

### Demo:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jccke8IHPJo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jccke8IHPJo)

## Problem / Background:

The current NFT market presents several key challenges that limit broader participation and sustainable growth.

**1. High Entry Barriers:**
    
    Blue-chip NFT projects such as BAYC, Azuki, and CryptoPunks are prohibitively expensive, making it difficult for most participants to access or invest in these highly sought-after assets.
    
**2. Illiquidity & Price Discovery Issues:**
    
    Most NFTs, built on the ERC-721 standard, are unique and non-fungible. This uniqueness, while valuable for collectors, creates liquidity problems, as it's harder to trade NFTs quickly and at fair market prices compared to fungible tokens like ETH or UNI.
    
**3. Inefficient Revenue Models:**
    
    Many NFT projects focus on merchandise sales and other limited revenue streams, overlooking the full potential of Web3 and DeFi integration that could provide more value to holders and project developers alike. We are creating a fractionalized liquidity hub that allows NFT holders to tokenize and split their NFTs into fractions. This approach significantly lowers the high entry barriers and enables more participants to own and trade fractionalized shares of premium NFTs. Additionally, by integrating these fractional NFTs with Uniswap natively, we enhance liquidity, enabling smoother price discovery and faster trading.

## Impact:

By addressing these core problems, our solution democratizes access to blue-chip NFTs, creating more opportunities for both investors and collectors. We aim to solve the liquidity challenges that plague the NFT market by providing a more flexible and efficient trading environment. Furthermore, NFT holders will have access to new revenue models beyond merchandise sales, offering sustainable income opportunities. This approach ultimately drives broader participation and paves the way for more innovative uses of NFTs in the Web3 ecosystem.

## Challenges:

This is our first time integrating Chainlink VRF and CCIP into a project, and we are very interested in these techniques and dedicate a significant amount of time to studying them. We face two main challenges: (1) the complex mathematics involved in Uniswap V4's swap and liquidity operations, and (2) local testing of Chainlink VRF and CCIP services, including the integration with the Hook::afterSwap callback. Thanks to incubator’s excellent tutorial, we are able to add several tests to modify liquidity and perform swap operations. Additionally, the rich learning resources provided by Chainlink help us understand how to test Chainlink VRF and CCIP. After weeks of exploration, we successfully integrate Chainlink services into the callback function, complete the related tests, and ensure a functional Proof of Concept.

## Extension:

**Different Pools**

Currently, we only support the ETH-gNFT pool, but we plan to add ERC20-gNFT pools in the future to increase ecosystem diversity.

**Expanded Callback Support**

We may introduce hooks related to liquidity provision and distribute rewards to incentivize LPs.

**Mode Selection**

In the current design, the gacha is triggered each time a user meets the threshold. We plan to offer users more options to choose between participating in the gacha or a standard swap.

**Custom Router**

We aim to develop our own router, replacing the default Uniswap router, with support for cross-chain functionality in the afterSwap function.

## Team:

Kevin Lin: Co-founder of Isle Finance and XueDAO
Louis Tsai: Web3 Security Researcher @Amber Group, Smart Contract Engineer @Isle Finance

It leverages Reactive Smart Contracts for decentralized execution and Filecoin for verifiable auditing, turning passive liquidity into an institutional-grade, market-neutral yield strategy.

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Liquidity Providers (LPs) currently face a "forced-selling" crisis known as Impermanent Loss and value extraction via Loss-versus-Rebalancing (LVR). This makes passive LPing a losing game during high volatility. We were inspired to build a "Sentinel" that turns Uniswap positions into risk-managed, delta-neutral instruments, allowing LPs to earn pure fee yield without market-direction risk.

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

I was inspired to build GammaHedge while reading a research paper on Loss-versus-Rebalancing (LVR). I discovered that by executing delta hedging in the exact opposite direction of pool liquidity movements, we could neutralize directional risk. GammaHedge solves the 'forced-selling' crisis of Impermanent Loss and the value extraction of LVR. We are transforming passive, risky LP positions into professionally managed, market-neutral yield instruments by automating the complex math required to stay delta-neutral.

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

GammaHedge is unique because it is a completely autonomous and fully on-chain sentinel. Unlike existing solutions that rely on centralized off-chain bots, we use Reactive Network to trigger rebalances directly on-chain. This makes institutional-grade risk management trustless and transparent. The impact is a safer Uniswap V4 ecosystem where LPs can provide liquidity to volatile pairs without fearing market crashes, effectively turning Uniswap into a stable 'Savings Account' powered by pure trading fees.

# Glyph

Description: Every AMM today charges a sandwich bot the same fee as a first-time user, because   pools have no memory. Glyph fixes that: a shared reputation registry that every v4 pool reads   before quoting a fee, repricing extractors up to 33x and paying the premium straight back to   LPs.
Tags: Cross-Chain, LP Fees, Unichain
Integrations: Reactive Network
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI8

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Reactive Network runs our cross-pool propagation: one RSC subscription to our registry covers
  every Glyph pool ever deployed, aggregates toxicity off-chain at zero gas cost to pools, and
  calls back to reprice a flagged wallet everywhere within seconds — deployed and funded on Lasna.
  Unichain hosts the stack on its canonical v4 PoolManager, and its one-second blocks are why our
  keeper repriced an attacker mid-burst rather than after. Brevis makes wallet history provable
  instead of asserted (ZK circuit + on-chain consumer feeding the scoring model). Pyth catches
  no-history attackers: anomalous first-touch price impact quotes the max fee instantly, and a
  stale feed never reverts a swap.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/jayteemoney/glyphh](https://github.com/jayteemoney/glyphh)
Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1q9Wxcj8WcIIy-kgZSbd4RTbaEaN11czOpiEvwezXt40/edit?usp=sharing
Project Link: https://glyphh-alpha.vercel.app/
Demo Video: [https://glyphh-alpha.vercel.app/](https://glyphh-alpha.vercel.app/)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

A sandwich bot pays the same fee on its thousandth attack as a retail user on their first swap pools have no memory, so LPs silently fund their own extraction (this is LVR, and on volatile pairs fees don't cover it). Every existing defense reacts to symptoms (price, volatility) instead of the actor, forgets between swaps, and defends one pool at a time while attackers simply rotate venues. Every mature market solves this with counterparty reputation; on-chain the data is public and unused. v4 hooks finally let a pool ask who is swapping before quoting a fee, Glyph is that answer. Decaying wallet reputation, fees up to 33x for extractors, premium back to LPs,  propagated to every pool in seconds.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Glyph is the only hook that prices the wallet behind the swap, and the only one where pools share what they learn;  flag a bot in one pool and every pool reprices it in seconds. Unlike volatility hooks that punish everyone when markets move, only extractors pay more (up to 33x), and the seven-day decay makes it a price, not a blacklist. It's live and measured: our detector flagged an attack bot mid-burst, 0 to 8,000, next swap 5.20% instead of 0.30%, premium to LPs in the same transaction. Impact: LVR stops being a silent tax on LPs and becomes their yield, deeper liquidity follows, and the registry underneath is a reusable reputation primitive such as;  lending, perps, and RFQ systems can read the same scores. Every new pool makes every other pool safer; no single-pool defense can say that.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hard parts only appeared live. Our LP-premium design called donate() after charging the dynamic fee. Every toxic swap reverted with CurrencyNotSettled, because v4's fee override already pays LPs and the donate double-counted; our tests missed it by pranking msg.sender but not tx.origin. Hook address mining failed because broadcasts deploy via the CREATE2 factory, not the EOA. Our block-based burst detection went blind on the real chain (receipt waits spread bursts across blocks), forcing a redesign around time-gaps and directional pressure, after which the keeper flagged the attacker mid-burst. Add trust-separating three score writers (EIP-712 nonces, hook allow-lists, validated Reactive callbacks) and surviving public infrastructure (lagging RPC nonces, the Kopli-to-Lasna migration), and most of the project was the gap between 'works in tests' and 'works.

# Glyph v2

Description: Glyph v2 is a Uniswap v4 hook that prices each swap by what it does to the pool, not by who sent it: a swap that closes the gap between    the pool and its reference price pays for the arbitrage it captures, while ordinary flow pays the base rate at any size, from any    wallet. And when a trader gets sandwiched, the attacker's surcharge is escrowed to that trader in the same transaction, rather than    handed to the LPs.
Tags: Dynamic Fee, LP Fees, LVR, MEV, Unichain
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI8

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Pyth supplies the reference price the directional premium is measured against, gated on staleness and confidence; Reactive Network  carries cross-pool toxicity on a single subscription that covers every pool we will ever deploy; and Uniswap v4's dynamic fees plus  afterSwapReturnDelta are what let the hook quote a per-swap price and route a sandwich surcharge to the victim — each one is  load-bearing, and removing any of them removes a named capability.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/jayteemoney/glyphh](https://github.com/jayteemoney/glyphh)
Slides: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/14cAfrpamHUR_rPThsKeIovvFbREwpMV-TLprJwUVyGw/edit?usp=sharing
Project Link: https://glyphh-alpha.vercel.app/
Demo Video: [https://www.loom.com/share/fbb3233904ea48708946922af10a447a](https://www.loom.com/share/fbb3233904ea48708946922af10a447a)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

  Passive liquidity is adversely selected. An LP makes one standing offer to everybody, but order flow is not homogeneous: informed traders only show up when the pool's price is stale, so the LP is on the losing side by construction. That is loss versus rebalancing, and on volatile pairs the standard fee tiers do not cover it. We measured it rather than asserting it. Over 30 days of real ETH/USD, a plain 0.30% pool let 45.6% of the gross arbitrage walk out, worth $188,209 on a $10M pool. A bot and a first time user pay the same fee, because the pool cannot tell them apart.

  Every defence we studied prices a proxy for this (volatility, order size, recent price drift), or it prices the sender. Proxies misfire
  in both directions, and pricing the sender fails the moment someone funds a new wallet.
                                 
  The inspiration was being told exactly that. Glyph competed at UHI9, and the judge wrote: "You key everything off tx.origin, which is 
  better than the router sender but still spoofable via fresh wallets, so I'd think about how a sandwicher simply rotating EOAs defeats 
  the score." He was right, and no better identity key fixes it; every key an attacker controls, they can mint more of. That objection
  forced the question this version is built on: not who sent this swap, but what does this swap do to the pool?

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Two of the three layers are new. The first is not, and saying so plainly is what makes the rest credible. Oracle divergence capture already exists: DetoxHook takes 70% of the arbitrage and donates it to LPs, and Nezlobin's directional fee reaches a similar place with no oracle at all. Ours is a refinement, using a 40 basis point threshold instead of roughly 2%, so the ordinary case is caught at all, and reading the pool's pre swap slot0 so a large swap cannot inflate the gap it is then charged for.

  What has no precedent we could find is the second layer. No deployed design routes a sandwich surcharge to the sandwiched trader, in the same transaction, funded by the attacker. Every other MEV hook charges the attacker more and hands the money to the LPs, who are not the party a sandwich harms. The third layer is also new: no v4 hook inverts reputation into a discount, so rotating a wallet no longer returns an attacker to free, it returns them to unproven, forfeiting trust that took real settled volume to earn.

  The composition is what holds it together. The layers are ordered by how much identity they need, and the first two need none, so sybilling the identity layer completely still leaves L1 and L2 firing at full strength.

  For impact, we replayed 30 days of real ETH/USD through the fee model. A Glyph pool keeps 82.4% of the gross arbitrage against 54.4% for a plain 0.30% pool, worth roughly $143,000 returned to LPs in a month on a $10M pool, and the capture ratio holds between 77% and 88% across a 25x range of pool size. The cost to everyone else is the number that actually decides whether this is worth deploying: 1.05% of ordinary swaps were misread as arbitrage, and no swap that widened the gap paid a premium at any size, from any wallet, which is guaranteed by construction and fuzz tested rather than merely observed.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hard part was not writing the mechanism. It was that almost every serious failure was silent: no revert, no error, just a wrong number or a feature that quietly did nothing.

  The first was inherited from v1. It derived a swap's price impact from params.sqrtPriceLimitX96, which is a slippage bound the swapper supplies and every router sets to the extreme tick. With oracle feeds configured, divergence saturated on every swap and honest retail read as maximally toxic, so the feature had to ship disabled. Nothing ever reverted. The bug was only visible by asking where the input came from rather than what it contained. v2 reads the pool's own slot0, so neither side of the comparison is controlled by the person paying the fee.

  The second we found by measuring rather than reasoning. Our arbitrage tolerance sat at 10 basis points, on the intuition that this represented oracle noise. Replaying 30 days of real prices showed it was surcharging 44% of ordinary swaps, because a pool's no arbitrage band is set by its base fee: below 30 basis points nobody arbitrages at all, so anything charged inside that band lands only on retail. We moved it to 40, collateral damage dropped to 1.5%, and we redeployed. A test now pins that threshold to BASE_FEE, so the reasoning that produced 10 cannot quietly come back.

  The third surfaced while rehearsing the demo. The sandwich rebate credited the victim zero, with no error and no event, because the attacker's toxicity had saturated across takes and the fee was already at the 10% cap, leaving no headroom to escrow. Each run now derives a fresh attacker.

  The common thread is that a mechanism which cannot announce its own failure has to be measured, not reasoned about. That is why the backtest exists, and why it is wired to the deployed arithmetic through a 2,500 vector parity test rather than to a reimplementation of it.

# Goldgard

Description: Goldgard is a hook that protects LST LP yield through oracle‑aware dynamic fees, circuit breaking and post‑swap delta rebalancing funded by a 0.02% insurance premium flowing into an ERC‑4626 Safety vault.
Tags: Cross-Chain, Dynamic Fee, LP Fees, LVR, Stablecoins, Yield Farming
Integrations: Reactive Network
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI9

**Key Links**

- **GitHub:** [https://github.com/jorshimayor/Goldgard/tree/main/goldgard-hookathon](https://github.com/jorshimayor/Goldgard/tree/main/goldgard-hookathon)
- **Demo Video:** [https://youtu.be/60bY2buG7YY](https://youtu.be/60bY2buG7YY)

**Partner Integrations**

Reactive Network makes Goldgard proactive instead of only reactive. The GoldgardReactiveWatcher contract on Lasna listens to OraclePriceUpdated events emitted on Sepolia. When TWAP vs Chainlink divergence crosses the early-warning threshold, it sends a callback back to Sepolia through GoldgardCallbackReceiver, which validates the callback path and tells the hook to raise an alert level — triggering fee adjustments before the hook's own local circuit breaker would fire.

**Problem / Background**

Liquid Staking Tokens (LSTs) yield a steady 3–7%, but depositing them into traditional AMMs to earn swap fees is a trap. Natural price drift triggers heavy Impermanent Loss (IL) and Loss Versus Rebalancing (LVR). This structural flaw routinely bleeds 8–15% of capital, completely wiping out the staking rewards LPs came to earn.

Hedging an active position forces users across separate protocols — external rebalancing managers, isolated lending platforms — inflicting massive gas fees and critical execution delays, exposing funds to toxic MEV bots and stale hedges.

**Impact**

Goldgard eliminates this friction as a self-contained yield-protection layer built directly into Uniswap v4's core architecture. A defensive beforeSwap hook monitors prices against external oracles, dynamically raising fees during volatility and tripping a circuit breaker if price de-pegs past 8%. An automated afterSwap hedging engine then measures directional drift and runs a counter-swap against an internal, protocol-owned Hedge Reserve to absorb the LVR.

The entire sequence executes via flash accounting using EIP-1153 transient storage — all balances settle to net-zero within a single transaction block, bypassing permanent storage writes and slashing traditional multi-contract gas costs by roughly 40%.

Three structural guarantees: (1) underlying staking yield is preserved — LST collateral continuously earns its baseline rewards without being wrapped or lent out; (2) the pool's aggregate delta is actively neutralized on every trade with no manual intervention required; (3) residual loss is backstopped by a protocol-owned ERC-4626 Safety Module funded by a 0.02% fee on every swap.

**Challenges**

Pre-v4 AMMs lacked the native capacity for atomic execution, which forced reliance on off-chain managers and multi-contract loops. The core challenge was compressing a full protection stack — oracle verification, user swaps, and aggregate delta rebalancing — directly into a single transaction lifecycle.

Taming the resulting gas overhead required studying EIP-1153 transient storage, with careful state management to ensure all balance deltas settled to net-zero via flash accounting before the lock closed.

Finally, ensuring the multi-layered defense system — dynamic fees, the internal Hedge Reserve, and the ERC-4626 Safety Module — interacted correctly without risking protocol insolvency was the hardest integration challenge.

# Gradient Shield

Description: A Uniswap v4 hook that makes sandwich attacks unprofitable on the very first trade — no reputation history needed — without ever blocking a trade. Measured against an identical unguarded pool, the attacker pays 5.3× more while the victim's execution and fee are completely unchanged.
Tags: LP Fees, MEV, Security, Trading Volume Rewards
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
Cohort: UHI10

## How did you integrate our partners, if any?

Uniswap v4: the whole project is a v4 hook — BaseHook, dynamic fees via OVERRIDE_FEE_FLAG so the PoolManager charges the escalated rate, CREATE2 address mining, and ERC-6909 multi-hop settlement.
EigenLayer: ServiceManagerBase and BLSSignatureChecker for the AVS, with BN254 aggregate-signature verification through the pairing precompile. The demo runs on a self-contained quorum using the identical construction, since the full middleware stack can't be deployed locally.

## What are the key links to share? (Ex. demo video, GitHub, deck)

Github: [https://github.com/sivajialla/gradient-shield#running-the-live-demo](https://github.com/sivajialla/gradient-shield#running-the-live-demo)
Slides: 
Project Link: 
Demo Video: [https://youtu.be/DQgjIuln4pw](https://youtu.be/DQgjIuln4pw)

## Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Sandwich bots extract value from traders, and reputation-based defences can't stop the first attack from a fresh wallet — which makes them easy to rotate around. Two problems emerged while building: reverting oversized trades stops sandwiches but breaks permissionlessness for honest traders, and Uniswap v4 hands hooks the router address rather than the trader's, so any per-address scoring silently penalises everyone behind a shared router. GradientShield prices the very first attack without blocking anyone, and resolves the real trader behind the router.

## Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Unique in three ways: it prices an attacker on their first trade with no reputation history, it penalises without ever excluding anyone, and it resolves the real trader behind the router — which most v4 hooks get wrong. Measured against an identical unguarded pool, the attacker's result goes from −0.011 to −0.059 ETH (5.3× worse) while the victim's execution and fee are unchanged, so honest flow pays nothing for the protection. The penalty is an LP fee, so extraction is redirected into LP yield rather than simply blocked.

## Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

The hardest bug looked like nothing: every test passed, but the hook detected nothing on a real chain. Detection state was in transient storage, which clears per transaction — and a sandwich is three transactions. Foundry hid it because a test function is one transaction. Moving to block-stamped persistent storage fixed it, with a vm.load regression test that can't see transient storage. Beyond that: the first design reverted oversized trades, which stopped sandwiches and honest large trades alike and had to be rebuilt around escalating fees; and v4 hands hooks a router rather than a trader, so 78 assertions across ten test files had encoded the wrong identity — two of them asserting the bug as intended behaviour.

# Problem / Background: What inspired the idea? What problems are you solving?

Stablecoin protocols like MakerDAO and HAI depend on external
  keepers and bots to update oracle prices, trigger rate
  adjustments, and maintain system health. This creates
  centralization risk, MEV extraction, and operational overhead —
  if keepers go offline, the protocol stalls. We asked: what if the
   protocol could maintain itself?

# Impact: What makes this project unique? What impact will this make?

Grinta is the first stablecoin protocol that embeds its entire
  oracle and PID rate controller directly inside a Uniswap V4 hook.
   Every swap automatically extracts the market price from trade
  deltas, fetches collateral pricing, and computes redemption rate
  adjustments — zero keepers, zero bots, zero external
  infrastructure. The protocol is alive as long as people trade.
  This is a new primitive: a self-maintaining, hook-native
  stablecoin where the AMM is the keeper.

# Challenges: What was challenging about building this project?

  Uniswap V4's unlock callback architecture meant we couldn't use
  standard liquidity or swap patterns — we had to build custom
  settlement flows from scratch. The 6-vs-18 decimal mismatch
  between USDC and GRIT required precise sqrtPriceX96 math that's
  easy to get catastrophically wrong (and we did, on the first
  pool). Fitting a full PI controller with leaky integrator into a
  gas-efficient hook callback, while maintaining WAD/RAY precision
  across the price extraction pipeline, pushed Solidity's stack
  limits and required careful function decomposition.

# HAYDENFLOW

Description: HaydenFlow is a programmable liquidity protocol that re-engineers the AMM for tokenized equities. It leverages on-chain correlation engines and intelligent multi-hop routing to slash impermanent loss and optimize trading yields.
Tags: LP Fees, Pool Native Incentivization, Stablecoins, Tokenized Stocks, Trading Volume Rewards, Unichain
Submission Type: Hook Incubator (UHI)
